etymology: From the parable of Luke 19, in which a nobleman gives ten servants a pound each to trade with until he returns.
biblical_def: The parable of the pounds, spoken by the Lord Jesus as He drew near Jerusalem, tells of a certain nobleman who went into a far country to receive a kingdom and to return. He called ten servants, delivered to each one pound, and said, Occupy till I come. His citizens hated him and sent a message, saying, We will not have this man to reign over us. When he returned, having received the kingdom, he called his servants to reckon: one had gained ten pounds, and was set over ten cities; another had gained five, and was set over five; but one had hid his pound in a napkin, calling his lord an austere man, and was condemned out of his own mouth, his pound given to him that had ten. And the rebellious citizens who would not have him reign were slain before him. The parable teaches the present absence and certain return of the King, the duty of His servants to trade faithfully with what He has entrusted until He comes, the reckoning that awaits all, the reward of faithful service, the judgment of the slothful, and the destruction of those who refuse His reign. The dictionary honors the parable of the pounds as the Lord’s charge to stewardship and watchfulness between His ascension and His return: occupy till I come.
webster_summary: The parable of Luke 19, in which a nobleman gives ten servants a pound each, saying, Occupy till I come; a charge to faithful stewardship until the King returns.

The rebellious citizens who refused his reign were destroyed.
scriptures: And he called his ten servants, and delivered them ten pounds, and said unto them, Occupy till I come.
And he said unto him, Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities.
And he saith unto him, Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee, thou wicked servant. Thou knewest that I was an austere man, taking up that I laid not down, and reaping that I did not sow:
But those mine enemies, which would not that I should reign over them, bring hither, and slay them before me.
corruption_summary: The parable is read as endorsing mere worldly enterprise or moralized into self-improvement; it teaches stewardship under the returning King and judgment on rebellion.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. One corruption reads the parable as a blessing on mere worldly enterprise and gain, as though the Lord commended financial ambition for its own sake; another moralizes it into a generic call to develop one’s potential. Both miss the King. The pounds are entrusted by a Lord who has gone to receive a kingdom and will return to reckon; the trading is service rendered to Him, and the gain is the increase of His interests, not the servant’s self-realization.

The principle to recover is stewardship under the absent but returning King. The command Occupy till I come (Luke 19:13) governs the whole age between the ascension and the second advent: the servants are to trade faithfully with what their Lord has given—gifts, gospel, opportunity—until He comes to reward the faithful with authority (Luke 19:17) and to judge the slothful out of his own mouth (Luke 19:22). And the parable ends in solemn warning: the citizens who said, We will not have this man to reign over us, are slain before him (Luke 19:27). To refuse the reign of Christ is to perish; to serve Him faithfully is to enter into His joy.

etymology: From the parable of Matthew 20, the labourers in the vineyard hired at different hours yet paid the same penny.
biblical_def: The parable of the labourers in the vineyard, in Matthew 20, tells of a householder who went out early to hire labourers for his vineyard, agreeing with them for a penny a day. He went out again at the third, sixth, ninth, and even the eleventh hour, hiring others and promising, Whatsoever is right I will give you. When evening came, he paid every man a penny, beginning with the last; and those hired first, receiving the same, murmured against the householder. But he answered one of them, Friend, I do thee no wrong: didst not thou agree with me for a penny? Take that thine is, and go thy way: I will give unto this last, even as unto thee. Is thine eye evil, because I am good? The parable teaches the sovereign freedom and goodness of God in dispensing His grace: He owes salvation to none, gives it freely to whom He will, and is not unjust to give the latecomer the same reward as the early servant. It rebukes the merit-seeking, comparing, envious spirit that would make grace a wage, and exalts the generosity of the God who saves the dying thief as freely as the lifelong saint. The dictionary honors this parable as a great picture of grace over against merit: the first shall be last, and the last first, for salvation is the gift of a good and sovereign God, not the payment of a debt.
webster_summary: The parable of Matthew 20; labourers hired at different hours yet paid the same penny, teaching the sovereign freedom and goodness of God in giving grace.

corruption_summary: The parable is read as a complaint about unfair wages or a charter for worldly equality; it teaches the sovereign, free goodness of God in giving grace, not a debt.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. One corruption reads the parable as a lesson in labour economics or fair wages, missing its subject entirely; another presses it into a charter for worldly equality of outcome. Both forget that the penny is grace, not a wage earned. The householder wrongs no one—those hired first received the very sum they agreed upon (Matt 20:13)—but he is free to be generous to the latecomer with what is his own.

The principle to recover is the sovereign freedom and goodness of God in salvation. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good? (Matt 20:15). God owes salvation to none and gives it freely to whom He will, having mercy on whom He will have mercy (Rom 9:15). The parable rebukes the merit-seeking, comparing, envious heart that would turn grace into a wage and resent the Lord’s generosity to others. It comforts the latecomer—the dying thief, the deathbed convert—with the same penny given to the lifelong saint, for the last shall be first, and the first last (Matt 20:16).

etymology: The command of the nobleman in the parable of the pounds (Luke 19:13); occupy in its older sense, to trade or do business.
biblical_def: Occupy till I come is the command of the nobleman in the parable of the pounds, given to his servants as he departed to receive a kingdom: he delivered them ten pounds, and said, Occupy till I come (Luke 19:13). The word occupy here carries its older English sense—to trade, to do business, to put to use—not the modern sense of merely holding a place. The servants were not told to bury their pounds or stand idle, but to employ their lord’s money in his service until his return. So the saying has become a watchword for the whole duty of the church between the ascension of Christ and His second coming: His servants are to trade faithfully with what He has entrusted—the gospel, their gifts, their time, their opportunities—not in idleness, not in mere preservation, but in active, fruitful labour for their absent Lord, looking for the reckoning at His return. It joins watchfulness to work: the King is coming, and His servants are to be found, not asleep, but trading. The dictionary honors occupy till I come as the marching order of the church militant: to labour diligently in the Master’s business until He returns to call His servants to account and to reward the faithful with authority and joy.
webster_summary: The nobleman’s command in the parable of the pounds; occupy meaning to trade, a watchword for faithful labour until the King returns.

corruption_summary: The phrase is read as mere holding-the-fort passivity; in its older sense it commands active, fruitful trading in the Master’s service until He comes.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is a misunderstanding bred by the change of the English word: occupy now suggests merely holding a position, sitting tight, keeping a seat warm. Read so, the command seems to counsel passivity—hold the fort until the Lord returns. But the older sense, plain in the parable, is to trade, to do business, to put the pound to fruitful use. The servant condemned in the parable was precisely the one who held his pound idle in a napkin.

The principle to recover is active, diligent labour for the absent Lord. The church is not to bury her talent or merely preserve what she has, but to trade with it—always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing her labour is not in vain (1 Cor 15:58), doing whatsoever she does heartily, as to the Lord (Col 3:23). And this labour is yoked to watchfulness, for the King is coming at an hour we know not (Matt 25:13). Occupy till I come is therefore no charter for idleness or mere survival, but the marching order of a working, watching church, that would be found trading when her Lord returns.

etymology: A biblical image of the separation of the righteous from the wicked, drawn from threshing (Matt 3:12; Psa 1:4).
biblical_def: Wheat and chaff is a recurring biblical image for the separation of the righteous from the wicked in the judgment of God. At the threshing floor the grain was beaten out, then tossed into the wind by the winnowing fan, so that the heavy kernels of wheat fell to be gathered into the garner, while the light, worthless chaff was carried off by the wind to be burned. John the Baptist used the figure of Christ: whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire. The Psalmist sets the same contrast: the ungodly are not so, but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away. The image teaches the certainty of a final, public, and irreversible separation: the wicked, however they flourish for a season, have no weight, no root, no abiding substance before God, and shall be driven away; the righteous, the true wheat of the Lord’s field, shall be gathered and kept. It warns against a religion that is all show and no substance, mere chaff that looks like grain until the wind of judgment proves it. The dictionary honors wheat and chaff as a solemn picture of the great division of the last day, when the Lord shall gather His own and the chaff shall be burned with fire unquenchable.

corruption_summary: The image is softened to deny final judgment or any real division; Scripture sets a certain and irreversible separation of the wheat from the chaff.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the modern softening that recoils from the image’s plain teaching of final judgment—the gathering of the wheat and the burning of the chaff with unquenchable fire. A sentimental religion would have all the grain saved and no chaff burned, denying the real and irreversible division that Scripture sets before us. But the Baptist’s words are not gentle: Christ will throughly purge His floor (Matt 3:12; Luke 3:17).

The principle to recover is the certainty and finality of the judgment’s separation, and the warning it carries against empty profession. The chaff looks like grain on the stalk; only the winnowing reveals its worthlessness. So a religion of mere outward show, without the weight of true grace and the root of saving faith, will be exposed when the wind of judgment blows. The ungodly, however they flourish, are like the chaff which the wind driveth away (Psa 1:4), as stubble before the storm (Job 21:18). The image summons every hearer to be true wheat—rooted, weighty, real—and not the chaff that the fire will consume.

etymology: The instrument used to toss threshed grain into the wind to separate wheat from chaff; a figure of divine judgment (Matt 3:12).
biblical_def: The winnowing fan was the instrument—a broad shovel or fork—used at the threshing floor to throw the beaten grain up into the wind, so that the breeze might carry away the light chaff and let the heavy wheat fall back to be gathered. John the Baptist took this familiar implement as a figure of the judgment that the coming Christ would execute: Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire. The fan in the hand of Christ signifies His office as Judge, who sifts and separates, discerning the true from the false, the genuine wheat of His people from the worthless chaff of the unbelieving and the hypocrite. The same Lord who came first in lowliness to save will come again in glory to judge, His fan in His hand to purge His floor thoroughly, leaving nothing unsifted. The image presses the searching nature of His judgment: no false profession will survive the wind, no hidden chaff escape the sifting. The dictionary honors the winnowing fan as an emblem of Christ the Judge, who will throughly purge His floor at the last day, and as a summons to self-examination, that we be found the true wheat and not the chaff which the fan casts to the fire.

corruption_summary: The fan’s imagery of sifting judgment is muted by a sentimental age; Scripture holds it up as the emblem of Christ the searching Judge.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the muting of the fan’s plain meaning by an age that would rather not speak of judgment. The winnowing fan is an instrument of separation, and the Baptist set it in the hand of Christ precisely to declare that He comes to sift—to gather the wheat and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire (Matt 3:12; Luke 3:17). To soften this is to silence the very note John was sent to sound before the Lord.

The principle to recover is the searching, dividing nature of Christ’s judgment, and the self-examination it demands. The fan in His hand will purge His floor throughly: nothing will be left unsifted, no false profession will survive the wind. The prophets had used the same figure of God fanning a faithless people (Jer 15:7; Isa 41:16). The image is therefore no idle terror but a mercy that warns: it summons every hearer, while there is time, to flee the wrath to come, to be made true wheat by grace, and to be gathered into the garner rather than cast to the fire.

etymology: From the saying of Christ in Matthew 5:26; the last and least coin, exacted to the full in judgment.
biblical_def: The uttermost farthing is the last and least coin named in the Lord’s warning in the Sermon on the Mount: Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him; lest at any time the adversary deliver thee to the judge, and the judge deliver thee to the officer, and thou be cast into prison. Verily I say unto thee, Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing. The farthing was a coin of the smallest value, and to pay the uttermost farthing is to discharge the very last and least of a debt, with nothing remitted. The Lord uses the image to press the urgency of reconciliation and the exactness of divine justice: the debtor cast into prison cannot come out until the whole debt, down to the last coin, is paid—and the sinner has no means to pay it. The saying drives home the perfect, exacting righteousness of God, which will not overlook the least transgression, and so the desperate need of the sinner for a Saviour who pays what he cannot. For the believer, Christ has paid the uttermost farthing of his debt upon the cross; for the impenitent, the prison-house of justice exacts payment that can never be made, and so the sentence is endless. The dictionary honors this saying as a window into the exactness of God’s justice and the fulness of Christ’s satisfaction.
webster_summary: The last and least coin in Christ’s warning (Matt 5:26); a figure of the exactness of divine justice, which remits nothing and must be fully paid.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the reduction of the saying to mere prudent counsel about settling disputes out of court, missing its deeper warning. The Lord does urge swift reconciliation, but the image of the debtor who cannot come out of prison till he has paid the uttermost farthing (Matt 5:26) opens upon the exactness of divine justice itself, which will not remit the least transgression unpaid.

The principle to recover is the perfect justice of God and the fulness of Christ’s satisfaction. The unforgiving servant was delivered to the tormentors till he should pay all that was due (Matt 18:34)—and a debt of ten thousand talents can never be paid in prison. So the sinner before God’s exact justice owes a debt he has no means to discharge; the prison-house exacts a payment endless because impossible. But here is the gospel: for the believer, Christ has paid the uttermost farthing, blotting out the handwriting that was against us, nailing it to His cross (Col 2:14), so that there is now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1). The exactness of justice magnifies the fulness of grace.

etymology: From the command of Christ in the Sermon on the Mount (Matt 5:34) and the echo of James (Jas 5:12).
biblical_def: Swear not is the Lord’s command in the Sermon on the Mount against the abuse of oaths and the careless, manipulative swearing of His day. The scribes had taught that oaths sworn by heaven, by the earth, by Jerusalem, or by one’s own head were less binding than those sworn by the name of God, and so had bred a culture of evasive, graded swearing meant to deceive. Against this the Lord said, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God’s throne: nor by the earth; for it is his footstool—for all such oaths invoke God whether they name Him or not. But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil. James repeats the charge: above all things, swear not. The command does not forbid the lawful, solemn oath taken before God in weighty matters—courts, covenants, the swearing that Scripture elsewhere permits and even God Himself employs—but it forbids the profane, rash, evasive, and habitual swearing that treats God’s name as a tool and truth as a thing to be manipulated. The disciple’s plain word is to be so true that his yea is yea without an oath to prop it. The dictionary honors swear not as the call to transparent truthfulness, the speech of those whose word, like their Master’s, needs no oath because it never lies.
webster_summary: Christ’s command against evasive and profane swearing; let your yea be yea and nay be nay, the plain truthfulness whose word needs no oath to prop it.

corruption_summary: The command is stretched to forbid all lawful oaths, or ignored to excuse profane speech; Christ forbids evasive and irreverent swearing and calls for plain truth.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two opposite errors attend the command. The first stretches Swear not at all to forbid every oath whatever, including the lawful, solemn oath taken before God in court or covenant—an oath that Scripture elsewhere permits, that the apostle Paul takes, and that God Himself condescends to swear. The second error ignores the command altogether and excuses the profane, careless taking of God’s name that fills common speech, in plain violation of the third commandment (Exo 20:7).

The principle to recover is transparent truthfulness as the mark of the disciple. The Lord’s target was the evasive, graded swearing of the scribes, who multiplied oaths precisely to deceive—and behind every such oath stands God, whether His name is spoken or not, for heaven is His throne and earth His footstool (Matt 5:34). The remedy is speech so honest that it needs no oath to prop it: let your communication be Yea, yea; Nay, nay (Matt 5:37; Jas 5:12). The Christian is to be a man of his word, whose plain yes and no can be trusted, because, like his Master, he does not lie.

etymology: From Paul’s charge in 1 Thessalonians 5:21, Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
biblical_def: Test all things—in the Authorized Version, Prove all things; hold fast that which is good—is Paul’s charge to the Thessalonians, set among his closing exhortations: Quench not the Spirit. Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. Abstain from all appearance of evil. To prove is to test, to assay, as metal is tried to discern whether it is true; the believer is not to receive every teaching, claim, or spirit uncritically, nor to reject them all in suspicion, but to examine them by the standard of God’s revealed word, retaining the good and refusing the evil. The charge guards against two opposite faults: the credulity that swallows every novelty and the cynicism that despises all prophesying. It assumes a fixed standard—the Scriptures—by which all things are weighed, for without a sure rule no true proving is possible. So John bids us try the spirits whether they are of God, and the noble Bereans searched the Scriptures daily to test even an apostle’s preaching. The dictionary honors this charge as the Christian’s duty of discernment: to bring every doctrine and claim to the touchstone of Scripture, holding fast what is proved good and abstaining from all appearance of evil, that the church be neither carried about by every wind of doctrine nor closed against the genuine work of God.
webster_summary: Paul’s charge to discernment—prove all things, hold fast that which is good—testing every teaching by the standard of Scripture, refusing both credulity and cynicism.

corruption_summary: The charge is twisted into open-minded relativism or a license for endless doubt; Scripture commands discernment by a fixed standard, holding fast the good and refusing the evil.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond one twist. The corruption is to wrench Prove all things into a charter for open-minded relativism—as though the believer must give every idea a hearing and settle on nothing, keeping an endlessly open mind. But Paul’s charge has a second half that the relativist drops: hold fast that which is good (1 Thess 5:21). The proving is not aimless; it aims at retaining the good and refusing the evil, and it assumes a fixed standard by which good and evil are known.

The principle to recover is discernment by the rule of Scripture. To prove all things is to assay them, as metal is tried, against the touchstone of God’s word—to the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, there is no light in them (Isa 8:20). So John bids us try the spirits whether they are of God (1 John 4:1), and the Bereans searched the Scriptures daily to test even Paul’s preaching (Acts 17:11). The charge cuts both ways: against the credulity that swallows every novelty, and against the cynicism that despises prophesying. The church is to weigh all, hold the good, and let the chaff go.

etymology: From the charge of 1 John 4:1, Try the spirits whether they are of God.
biblical_def: Try the spirits is the apostle John’s charge to discernment: Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world. Behind every teacher stands a spirit—either the Spirit of truth or the spirit of error—and the believer is not to credit every claim of inspiration or revelation, but to test it. John gives the touchstone: every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God, and every spirit that confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is not of God; and this is that spirit of antichrist. The test is doctrinal and Christological: a true confession of the incarnate Christ, His true deity and true humanity, marks the Spirit of God; its denial unmasks the spirit of antichrist, however spiritual or miraculous the claimant may appear. The charge assumes that not every supernatural or religious claim is of God, that error often clothes itself in the language of the Spirit, and that the church must discern by the apostolic standard. The dictionary honors this charge as the believer’s defense against false prophets and seducing spirits: to test every teaching and claimed revelation by the confession of Christ revealed in Scripture, refusing the spirit of error however fair its appearance, and holding fast the Spirit of truth.
webster_summary: John’s charge to test every spirit and teacher by the confession of Christ come in the flesh; the Spirit of truth confesses Him, the spirit of antichrist denies Him.

corruption_summary: The charge is set aside by a credulous hunger for the supernatural, or reduced to mere subjective discernment; John gives an objective, Christological test.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the credulous hunger, ancient and modern alike, that credits every claim of the spiritual, the miraculous, or the prophetic without testing it—the very thing John forbids. A church starved for the supernatural will believe any spirit that promises power or experience, forgetting that many false prophets are gone out into the world (1 John 4:1) and that the wolf comes in sheep’s clothing (Matt 7:15).

The principle to recover is the objective, Christological standard of John’s test. He does not leave us to a vague subjective discernment but gives a definite touchstone: every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God, and every spirit that denies the incarnate Christ is the spirit of antichrist (1 John 4:2-3). The test is doctrinal—the true confession of Christ’s deity and humanity—and it cuts through every appearance of spirituality and power. The church is therefore to try the spirits not by their fervor or their wonders but by their confession of the Christ revealed in Scripture, holding fast the Spirit of truth and refusing the spirit of error.

etymology: From the Olivet Discourse, Matthew 24:12, where Christ foretells that the love of many shall wax cold.
biblical_def: Love waxing cold is the Lord’s solemn prophecy in the Olivet Discourse concerning the days before His coming: And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold. To wax cold is to grow chill, as a fire dies down; and the love spoken of is that fervent love to God and to the brethren which marks the true disciple. The Lord foretells that as iniquity abounds—as lawlessness multiplies, deceivers arise, and tribulation presses—the love of many professors will cool, their first ardor fading into formality, indifference, and self-love. It is a chilling word, for it speaks not of the world’s coldness, which is no surprise, but of the cooling of love among those who once seemed warm. Yet the Lord adds the promise that holds the faithful: But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. The prophecy is therefore both warning and comfort: warning against the deadening effect of abounding sin upon the heart’s love, and the call to watchfulness lest our own love grow cold; comfort in the assurance that true grace perseveres, and that the enduring love of the elect shall not finally fail. The dictionary honors this saying as a searching word for a lawless age, a summons to keep the fire of love burning, and a call to the perseverance by which the saints are kept.
webster_summary: Christ’s prophecy that as iniquity abounds the love of many shall wax cold; a warning to watchfulness, with the promise that he who endures to the end shall be saved.

corruption_summary: The saying is treated as mere ancient pessimism or ignored amid abounding sin; Christ warns against cooling love and calls the saints to watchful perseverance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the dismissal of the saying as mere ancient pessimism, or the failure to heed it amid abounding iniquity. The Lord’s word is precise and searching: it speaks not of the cold world, whose hostility is expected, but of the cooling of love among professors—the dying down of a fire once warm, as lawlessness multiplies and tribulation presses. To ignore this is to be unwatchful precisely where the danger lies.

The principle to recover is twofold: the deadening power of abounding sin upon love, and the perseverance of true grace. Where iniquity abounds, the love of many waxes cold (Matt 24:12); even a true church may leave her first love (Rev 2:4), and so the disciple is called to watchfulness, to consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works (Heb 10:24), and to keep the fire burning lest his own love grow chill. Yet the saying ends in hope: he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved (Matt 24:13). The love that perseveres is the mark of the elect, kept by the power of God; the warning drives the saint to watch, and the promise assures him he shall be kept.
